newsitem.title: GERMANY: German states criticised for forcing Bosnians home.
newsitem.headline: German states criticised for forcing Bosnians home.

text.p: A cross-party group of politicians including the government's commissioner for foreigners' affairs called on Germany's federal states on Wednesday to soften their policy of forcibly repatriating refugees who fled the war in Bosnia.

As interior ministers of the 16 states prepared for a two-day meting in Bonn starting on Thursday, the commissioner, Cornelia Schmalz-Jacobsen, called on them to suspend deportation while the policy was reviewed.
"The aim... cannot be to send back the refugees, who were taken in by Germany in such an exemplary way, with no consideration for the situation there," she wrote in a statement.

Germany took in around 320,000 Bosnian refugees -- more than the rest of the European Union combined -- but the cash-strapped states decided to start forcible repatriations last year after few returned voluntarily.

So far the main criterion for repatriation has been family situation, with single adults being asked to go first, even though this may mean Moslems facing a choice between returning to a homeland now run by hostile Serbs or moving to a temporary shelter in another part of Bosnia.

But six leading politicians, including the former EU administrator in the Bosnian city of Mostar, Hans Koschnick, said in a letter to the ministers that refugees should be selected according to ethnicity and origin.
"It is impossible for people of Croatian or Moslem ethnicity, who come from what is now the Bosnian Serb Republic of Serbia, to go back there," Schmalz-Jacobsen added.

Kerstin Mueller, opposition Greens parliamentary spokeswoman, said that "these repatriation measures -- without considering the situation there -- massively endanger the fragile peace process and are therefore irresponsible".
The conservative southern state of Bavaria has forcibly returned the most refugees -- 121 -- since the policy started.

Germany's policy of allowing forced repatriations has also drawn criticism from refugee agencies, which say it risks further destabilising the already chaotic conditions in Bosnia after the 1992-95 war.
Sources close to the interior ministers' conference said they thought a policy change was unlikely, although repatriations could be slowed down.

Defence Minister Volker Ruehe told German television that the more refugees returned to rebuild the country, the better were the chances of a lasting peace. He said German soldiers could protect returnees if necessary.
